messages.subject: Effects versus means
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

Having absorbed your wisdom passively the past couple years, I need to ask
a specific question.

In a recent experiment of mine with a 4x2x2 design, I found some
significant effects on a consistency variable, where the participants saw
either the same word (e.g. "rotates") repeatedly in a block or a word
randomly selected from four (i.e. "rotates," "shrinks," "expands," or
"fades"). That is, after trying to maximize my random effects structure, I
found that the (binary, centered) consistency fixed effect was significant.
Unfortunately, when I look at the means for this effect, they go in the
correct direction for one level of SOA, but in the opposite direction (i.e.
not the direction indicated by the significance) for the other level of
SOA. There was no interaction.

The model is telling me something different than the means. I was under the
impression that this was a possible consequence of the estimation of random
effects, but my dissertation committee is not convinced. Can any of you
offer any advice on how to interpret this situation? I'm happy to offer any
more detail, and talk about some of the things I've investigated. My hope
is that I've overlooked something simple, so please don't hesitate to tell
me so!

Best,
Jason

messages.subject: Re: Effects versus means
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,
Depending on whether the factors are all interacting and on the contrasts
you are using, the effect can reflect different comparisons.

It will help if you paste the model output and say what contrasts you used
for every variable.

If all predictors are sum-coded or centered, I would interpret it as a
"main effect" of consistency, i.e., across levels of SOA.

If you want to know the effect for each SOA, it could be better if you used
treatment contrasts or if you fit a separate model to the data in each SOA.

Hope this helps,
João

messages.subject: Re: Effects versus means
messages.body_plain:
Here’s another possible explanation for the discrepancy between the
model and the means.  You didn’t mention what your dependent variable
was but if it was a reaction time and if your dependent variable was
log-transformed in the analysis (as is commonly done) the discrepancy
may be due to the fact that the model evaluates the data on the log
scale but your means are calculated on the original scale (milliseconds
or whatever).  Depending on the distribution of the reaction times in
the conditions, the pattern of the means can look differently on the log
and the original scale.  For instance, if you have some really long
reaction times in one condition, they will have a big impact on the
original scale but a smaller impact on the log scale.  I know that it’s
common to report arithmetic means of reaction times even when the data
was analyzed on the log scale but geometric means (basically the mean on
the log-scale back-transformed to the original scale) may actually make
more sense in these situations.

   Titus

messages.subject: Re: ordinal response - lmer
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paraskevi,

I don’t think lmer can be used.  The standard solution for this kind of
data is ordered logistic regression.  I recently analyzed a similar data
set (1–7 Likert scale) and I played with the function `polr' in the
package MASS.  For some reason, I forgot what it was, I decided against
using this function but implemented something similar in Stan (using
ordered_logistic).  However, the reason why I decided against using it
may not be relevant for your purposes.  Apparently the R package
MCMCglmm can also be used for ordered logistic regression but I haven’t
tried that.

If you pre-aggregate the data on some level (items or subjects), you can
also run a beta regression (after scaling the data to the interval
[0,1]).  The R package betareg provides the necessary tools.  However,
there is a longstanding debate about whether or not beta regression is
appropriate for this kind of data.  It’s potentially more powerful but
makes assumptions that may not hold in your data.

- http://www.voteview.com/R_Ordered_Logistic_or_Probit_Regression.htm
- Cribari-Neto, F., & Zeileis, A. (2009). Beta regression in R.
- http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/index.html

Hope that helps.

  Titus

On 2015-04-23 Thu 09:39, Paraskevi Argyriou wrote:
> Dear all,

> If not, could anyone suggest a paper/chapter using the ordinal package?
>
> Many thanks
